To reduce vignette build time, most code chunks are displayed but not evaluated
during package compilation. Only the chunks that load and inspect the bundled
toy datasets are run.

```{r library, eval=TRUE}
library(clinprog)
```

## Overview

clinprog is an R package for identifying and evaluating prognostic molecular
signatures (genes/transcripts) using bootstrap-based penalized LASSO Cox regression.

The package is organized into three main workflows:

- Module I: molecular signature discovery (`run_regression()`)
- Module II: survival analysis (`run_survival()`)
- Complete workflow (`run_complete()`)

In Module I, each bootstrap iteration fits a LASSO Cox model on a random subset of
features (`group_size`). Iterations whose subset contains too many highly correlated
features (`percentage_filter`) are discarded. The coefficients are then averaged
across iterations, and only features whose average coefficient passes a minimum
threshold are kept in the signature.

This vignette provides a brief step-by-step guide to running the clinprog pipeline and
exploring its outputs.

---

## Input data

### Expression and survival data

The main input must be a `data.frame` containing (in this order):

- Survival status (`OS`; 1 = event/dead, 0 = alive/censored)
- Survival time (`OS.time`)
- Expression values (genes or transcripts)

Each row represents a sample, and each column represents a molecular feature.
Sample identifiers are stored as row names. Expression values may be raw or
already log2(exp+1)-transformed; set `norm_exp = TRUE` when the values are raw
and clinprog should apply the log2(exp+1) transformation (see
[Choosing parameters](#choosing-parameters)).

The package bundles simulated toy datasets (not derived from any real patient data)
with 150 samples:

- `toy_gene_expression`: 53 genes
- `toy_transcript_expression`: 52 transcripts
- `toy_clinics`: 5 binary clinical variables

They are available as raw files and as ready-to-use objects. To read the raw
files, use `read_table()`, which uses the first column as row names:

```{r load-raw, eval=TRUE}
gene_file <- system.file("extdata", "toy_gene_expression.tsv", package = "clinprog")

toy_data <- read_table(gene_file)

head(toy_data[, 1:5])
```

Alternatively, the built-in object can be loaded directly:

```{r load-builtin, eval=TRUE}
data(toy_gene_expression)

head(toy_gene_expression[, 1:5])
```

Example structure (sample IDs as row names):

```text
             OS   OS.time   Gene1    Gene2    Gene3
Sample1      1    1200      52.30    3.10     0.00
Sample2      0    980       24.40    1.80     0.50
```

The toy data contain known, planted structure: genes `TOYRISK1-8` are higher and
`TOYPROT1-8` lower in patients with worse prognosis, so they are expected to
appear in the signature (with positive and negative coefficients, respectively).
The same holds for the transcripts `MSTRG.9001.*` and `MSTRG.9002.*`.

---

### Molecular signature

The `signature` argument used in `run_survival()` can be provided as:

- A `clinprog_signature` object generated by `run_regression()`
- A user-defined `data.frame`

(`run_complete()` passes the signature from the regression step automatically.)

The signature should contain (in this order) at least the following two mandatory columns:

- The features, either genes or transcripts (`feature`)
- Their respective coefficients from a regression survival analysis (`coefficient`)

Example structure:

```text
feature        coefficient
ENST00001      0.231
ENST00002     -0.412
ENST00003      0.118
```

A signature stored in a tab-separated file can be imported with `read_table()`
(see [Import utilities](#import-utilities)).

---

### Clinical data for multivariate analysis

When `run_multivariate = TRUE` in `run_survival()` or `run_complete()`, an additional
clinical `data.frame` must be provided using the `clinical_data` argument.

The clinical table should contain:

- Sample identifiers (row names) matching the expression table
- Binary (mandatory) clinical covariates suitable for multivariate Cox regression

```{r load-clin, eval=TRUE}
clin_file <- system.file("extdata", "toy_clinics.tsv", package = "clinprog")

clin_data <- read_table(clin_file)

head(clin_data)
```

Alternatively, the built-in object can be loaded directly:

```{r load-clin-builtin, eval=TRUE}
data(toy_clinics)

head(toy_clinics)
```

Example structure (sample IDs as row names):

```text
             Age    Gender   Race        Histotype            Grade
Sample1      Low    Female   White       Astrocytoma          G2
Sample2      High   Male     Not white   Oligodendroglioma    G3
```

---

## Choosing parameters {#choosing-parameters}

A few parameters have a large impact on the results:

| Parameter | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `norm_exp` | `FALSE` | Set to `TRUE` for raw expression values (applies log2(exp+1)). The minimum coefficient threshold is only reachable on the log scale for typical gene values (hundreds to thousands). |
| `feature_type` | `"gene"` | `"gene"` or `"transcript"`. It sets the minimum average coefficient to keep a feature (about 0.0035 for genes and 0.011 for transcripts). |
| `bootstrap` | `1` | Number of bootstrap iterations. A single iteration depends strongly on which features are randomly drawn, so use more iterations (the toy examples use 30) for any real analysis. |
| `group_size` | `10` | Number of features drawn per iteration. If fewer features than `group_size` remain after filtering, clinprog runs a single regression instead of the bootstrap. |
| `variance_filter` | `0.01` | Removes features whose variance (of the values divided by the column maximum, after the log2 transformation when `norm_exp = TRUE`) is below this value. |
| `percentage_filter` | `0.3` | Discards iterations in which this proportion of feature pairs is highly correlated. |
| `skip_survival_checks` | `FALSE` | Overrides the filtering steps related to survival assumptions (it replaces the former `force` argument). Keeping the default is recommended for real data. The toy datasets were validated with `skip_survival_checks = TRUE`. |
| `n_cores` | `1` | Number of cores used for the bootstrap. |
| `seed` | `123` | Random seed, stored in the returned object for reproducibility. |

Output files (plots, tables, JSON, RDS, reports, logs) are written using the prefix
given in `output_prefix`. To keep the examples below from writing into the working
directory, we use a temporary directory:

```{r out-dir, eval=TRUE}
out_dir <- tempdir()
```

---

## Module I - Molecular signature discovery

The `run_regression()` function identifies robust molecular signatures using filtering steps,
feature selection, and bootstrap LASSO Cox regression.

```{r run-regression}
reg_result <- run_regression(
  data = toy_gene_expression,
  output_prefix = file.path(out_dir, "my_analysis"),
  norm_exp = TRUE,
  bootstrap = 30,
  group_size = 10,
  percentage_filter = 0.3,
  variance_filter = 0.01,
  max_follow_up = NULL,
  feature_type = "gene",
  min_signature_size = NULL,
  min_signature_cutoff = NULL,
  skip_survival_checks = TRUE,
  save_plots = TRUE,
  save_table = TRUE,
  save_json = TRUE,
  save_rds = TRUE,
  report_format = FALSE,
  verbose = 1,
  n_cores = 1,
  seed = 123,
  save_log = TRUE
)
```

For reproducible analyses, the random seed is controlled by the `seed` parameter
(default `123`).

When `save_plots = TRUE` and/or `save_table = TRUE`, clinprog automatically exports plots and
result tables using `output_prefix`. If these options are disabled (default),
users can manually generate specific outputs using the visualization and export helper functions,
as specified at the end of each workflow section.

Users can also export metadata information in JSON format, such as the parameters used,
when `save_json = TRUE`. If this option is disabled (default), users can manually generate the file
using the specific helper function, specified later in this tutorial.

Similarly, users can export a summary report (in PDF or HTML) of the entire clinprog pipeline
by setting `report_format = "PDF"` or `report_format = "HTML"` (`TRUE` selects PDF).
If this option is disabled (default), users can manually produce the report using the
specific helper function, specified later in this tutorial.

Additionally, users can save the LOG of the entire clinprog pipeline when `save_log = TRUE`.
If this option is disabled (default), users can manually recover the LOG using the specific helper
function, specified later in this tutorial. This is independent of the `verbose` parameter,
which controls whether messages are printed to the terminal (`0`/`FALSE` to silence them).

Finally, users can save the results of a specific analysis in an RDS file when `save_rds = TRUE`.
If this option is disabled (default), users can manually save (and load) the results generated
by clinprog using the specific helper functions specified later in this tutorial.

---

## Finding the most parsimonious signature

When `min_signature_size` is provided (e.g., `min_signature_size = 2`), clinprog performs a
**top-k prefix search** to identify the smallest subset of features from the full signature that
still yields a statistically significant univariate log-rank test. Note that `min_signature_cutoff`
only has an effect when `min_signature_size` is also set.

### How it works

The algorithm proceeds as follows:

1. **Ranking**: Features from the full signature are already ordered by decreasing absolute coefficient value
(`|coefficient|`), as returned by the bootstrap + LASSO Cox regression step.
2. **Prefix evaluation**: Starting from `min_signature_size` (the minimum number of features to consider),
clinprog evaluates progressively larger prefixes of this ranked list. For each prefix of size `k`:
    - A clinprog score is computed using only the top-`k` features and their coefficients.
    - Patients are split into low/high score groups using the strategy defined by `min_signature_cutoff`
    (one of `"median"`, `"mean"`, `"signal"`, or `"roc"`).
    - A univariate Cox model is fitted, and the log-rank p-value is extracted.
3. **Stopping rule**: The search stops at the **first** `k` whose log-rank p-value drops below `0.05`.
That prefix is returned as the "minimal signature". If no prefix reaches significance, the full signature
is returned with a warning.

### Important considerations

This procedure is a **heuristic for parsimony**. Key notes:

- **In-sample selection**: The cutoff `p < 0.05` is applied on the same dataset used to derive the signature,
so the resulting p-value is optimistic. There is no correction for multiple testing across the `k` values tested.
- **Ordering dependency**: Because features are ranked by LASSO coefficient magnitude rather than univariate p-value,
a feature with a large multivariate weight but weak individual signal will still be included if it appears
early in the ranking.
- **Minimum, not optimal**: The procedure returns the smallest significant subset, not the subset with the
best predictive performance.

Users are encouraged to treat the minimal signature as a good starting point for further investigation,
not as a final validated model.

### Example usage

```{r run-regression-min}
reg_result_min <- run_regression(
  data = toy_gene_expression,
  output_prefix = file.path(out_dir, "my_analysis_min"),
  norm_exp = TRUE,
  bootstrap = 30,
  min_signature_size = 2,
  min_signature_cutoff = "median",
  skip_survival_checks = TRUE,
  seed = 17
)

# Compare the number of features
nrow(reg_result$signature)      # full signature
nrow(reg_result_min$signature)  # minimal signature

# Check which features remained
head(reg_result$signature)      # full signature
head(reg_result_min$signature)  # minimal signature
```

---

## Inspecting regression results

The result is an S3 object of class `clinprog_signature`.

```{r inspect-regression}
summary(reg_result)
print(reg_result)
as.data.frame(reg_result)
coef(reg_result)
plot(reg_result)
```

With the toy data, the signature is expected to contain several `TOYRISK*` genes
(positive coefficients) and `TOYPROT*` genes (negative coefficients). A few background genes
may also appear, because the minimum coefficient threshold is low.

---

## Regression visualization utilities

Plots can also be generated manually:

```{r regression-plots}
plot_histogram(reg_result$signature, output_prefix = file.path(out_dir, "my_histogram"))

plot_lollipop(reg_result$signature, output_prefix = file.path(out_dir, "my_lollipop"))
```

---

## Module II - Survival analysis

The `run_survival()` function applies a molecular signature to survival data and performs univariate
and optional multivariate survival analyses.

```{r run-survival}
surv_result <- run_survival(
  data = toy_gene_expression,
  signature = reg_result,
  output_prefix = file.path(out_dir, "my_survival"),
  norm_exp = TRUE,
  run_multivariate = TRUE,
  clinical_data = toy_clinics,
  score_cutoff = "roc",
  variance_filter = 0.01,
  max_follow_up = NULL,
  p_value_cutoff = 0.2,
  bootstrap = 100,
  skip_survival_checks = TRUE,
  save_plots = TRUE,
  save_table = TRUE,
  save_json = TRUE,
  save_rds = TRUE,
  report_format = FALSE,
  verbose = 1,
  save_log = TRUE
)
```

The score cutoff (`score_cutoff`) can be `"median"` (default), `"mean"`, `"signal"` or `"roc"`.
In the multivariate analysis, `p_value_cutoff` controls which clinical covariates are
carried over from the univariate step, and `bootstrap` sets the number of bootstrap iterations
for the multivariate model.

---

## Using the ROC curve to group scores

When `score_cutoff = "roc"` is specified, clinprog chooses the score threshold that best separates patients
into low/high risk groups using a ROC analysis.

### How the cutoff is determined

1. **Direction inference**: `survivalROC::survivalROC()` is used to compute a time-dependent ROC curve for
the continuous clinprog score, using the survival time (`OS.time`), the event status (`OS`) and the median
follow-up time as the prediction time point. The estimation method is **Nearest Neighbor Estimation (NNE)**,
with a span parameter of `0.25 * n^(-0.20)`. Its area under the curve (AUC) is used only to decide the direction
of the score: if AUC < 0.5, the direction is flipped so that higher scores consistently indicate higher risk.
2. **Optimal cutoff**: `OptimalCutpoints::optimal.cutpoints()` is applied to the score and the event status
using the **Youden index** (`sensitivity + specificity - 1`) to identify the score value that maximizes the
sum of sensitivity and specificity. The direction is set based on the one inferred in step 1.
3. **Group assignment**: Patients with scores above the cutoff are classified as "high"
(reference group in Cox models), and those at or below as "low".

### Important considerations

- **Time-dependence**: Only the direction of the score depends on the time-dependent ROC at the median follow-up
time. The cutoff itself is the Youden-optimal value for the event status, without a time horizon.
Users with specific time horizons may prefer to define a cutoff manually.
- **In-sample selection**: The cutoff is optimized on the same data used to evaluate the groups, so the resulting
group separation is optimistic. Consider `"median"` for a data-independent alternative.

### Example usage

```{r run-survival-roc}
surv_result_roc <- run_survival(
  data = toy_gene_expression,
  signature = reg_result,
  output_prefix = file.path(out_dir, "my_survival_roc"),
  norm_exp = TRUE,
  score_cutoff = "roc",
  skip_survival_checks = TRUE
)

# Inspect the ROC result
surv_result_roc$roc_result$cutoff
surv_result_roc$roc_result$auc
surv_result_roc$roc_result$direction
```

---

## Inspecting survival results

The result is an S3 object of class `clinprog_survival`.

```{r inspect-survival}
summary(surv_result)
print(surv_result)
as.data.frame(surv_result)
coef(surv_result)
plot(surv_result)
```

## Survival visualization utilities

Additional survival-related plots can also be generated manually. Below are a few examples:

```{r survival-plots-1}
plot_boxplot(data = surv_result$expression_data, signature = surv_result$signature,
             output_prefix = file.path(out_dir, "my_box"))

plot_scatter(data = surv_result$expression_data, signature = surv_result$signature,
             output_prefix = file.path(out_dir, "my_scatter"))

plot_wordcloud(data = surv_result$expression_data, signature = surv_result$signature,
               output_prefix = file.path(out_dir, "my_wcloud"))
```

```{r survival-plots-2}
plot_barplot_score(data = surv_result$expression_data,
                   score_cutoff_value = surv_result$score_cutoff_value,
                   output_prefix = file.path(out_dir, "my_score-bar"))

plot_lineplot_score(data = surv_result$expression_data,
                    score_cutoff_value = surv_result$score_cutoff_value,
                    output_prefix = file.path(out_dir, "my_line"))
```

```{r survival-plots-3}
# Use is_multi = TRUE when the PH test comes from a multivariate model
plot_ph(x = surv_result$ph_result,
        is_multi = !is.null(surv_result$survival$multivariate),
        output_prefix = file.path(out_dir, "my_ph"))

uni <- surv_result$survival$univariate$table
plot_km(data = surv_result$expression_data,
        score_cutoff_value = surv_result$score_cutoff_value,
        p_value = paste0("p = ", uni$log.rank.pvalue, "\nHR: ", uni$hazard.ratio),
        output_prefix = file.path(out_dir, "my_km"))

plot_swimmer(data = surv_result$expression_data,
             score_cutoff_value = surv_result$score_cutoff_value,
             facet_by = "score_group",
             output_prefix = file.path(out_dir, "my_swim"))
```

If ROC was used to define the score cutoff:

```{r survival-plots-roc}
plot_roc(x = surv_result$roc_result, output_prefix = file.path(out_dir, "my_roc"))
```

If multivariate analysis is performed:

```{r survival-plots-multi}
plot_forest(model_object = surv_result$survival$multivariate$model,
            output_prefix = file.path(out_dir, "my_forest"))

plot_clinics(data = surv_result$clinical_data, output_prefix = file.path(out_dir, "my_clin-box"))
```

If bootstrap resampling was performed during multivariate analysis:

```{r survival-plots-boot}
plot_barplot(plot_df = surv_result$survival$boot_table, type = "absolute",
             bootstrap = 100, output_prefix = file.path(out_dir, "my_bar"))
```

## Complete workflow

The `run_complete()` function sequentially runs both clinprog modules:

1. Molecular signature discovery
2. Survival analysis

The molecular signature generated during the regression step is automatically passed to the survival module.

```{r run-complete}
complete_result <- run_complete(
  data = toy_gene_expression,
  output_prefix = file.path(out_dir, "my_complete_analysis"),
  norm_exp = TRUE,
  bootstrap = 30,
  group_size = 10,
  percentage_filter = 0.3,
  variance_filter = 0.01,
  max_follow_up = NULL,
  feature_type = "gene",
  min_signature_size = NULL,
  min_signature_cutoff = NULL,
  run_multivariate = TRUE,
  clinical_data = toy_clinics,
  score_cutoff = "roc",
  p_value_cutoff = 0.2,
  skip_survival_checks = TRUE,
  save_plots = TRUE,
  save_table = TRUE,
  save_json = TRUE,
  save_rds = TRUE,
  report_format = FALSE,
  verbose = 1,
  n_cores = 1,
  seed = 123,
  save_log = TRUE
)
```

The parameters `norm_exp`, `bootstrap`, `variance_filter`, `max_follow_up`, and `seed` are applied to both
modules, although they may operate differently during the regression and survival analysis steps.

---

## Inspecting complete workflow results

The result is an S3 object of class `clinprog_complete`.

```{r inspect-complete}
summary(complete_result)
print(complete_result)
coef(complete_result)
plot(complete_result)
```

Module-specific results can also be accessed directly:

```{r complete-modules}
complete_result$regression

complete_result$survival
```

## Import utilities {#import-utilities}

clinprog provides a helper function for importing tabular data. By default, the first column is
used as row names:

```{r import}
my_expression <- read_table("path/to/expression_file.tsv")
my_signature  <- read_table("path/to/signature.txt", row_names = FALSE)
my_clinics    <- read_table("path/to/clinical_file.tsv")
```

Because `run_regression()`, `run_survival()` and `run_complete()` require `data.frame` inputs,
files must be imported first with `read_table()` (or any other reader that produces a `data.frame`
with sample IDs as row names).

---

## Export utilities

The package also provides helper functions for exporting results.

### Molecular signatures

```{r export-signature}
write_signature(reg_result, file.path(out_dir, "my_signature.txt"))
```

### Calculated scores

```{r export-score}
write_score(surv_result, file.path(out_dir, "my_scores.tsv"), include_clinical = TRUE)
```

### Univariate survival results

```{r export-uni}
write_univariate(surv_result, file.path(out_dir, "my_uniCox.txt"))
```

### Multivariate survival results

```{r export-multi}
write_multivariate(surv_result, file.path(out_dir, "my_multiCox.txt"))
```

### JSON with parameters and additional execution metadata

```{r export-json}
write_metadata(module = "run_complete",
               output_prefix = file.path(out_dir, "my_json"),
               parameters = list(norm_exp = TRUE, bootstrap = 30, seed = 123),
               command = "none")
```

### PDF/HTML clinprog report

```{r export-report}
write_report(object = complete_result, format = "PDF", author = "Dr. Your Name",
             file = file.path(out_dir, "my_report.pdf"))
```

## Returned S3 object structure

### Molecular signature object

```{r str-regression}
str(reg_result)
```

Typical objects contain:

- `signature`
- `plots`
- `params`
- `metadata`
- `call`

---

### Survival analysis object

```{r str-survival}
str(surv_result)
```

Typical objects contain:

- `signature`
- `score_cutoff_value`
- `expression_data`
- `clinical_data`
- `survival` (a list with `univariate`, `multivariate` and `boot_table`)
- `roc_result`
- `ph_result`
- `plots`
- `params`
- `metadata`
- `call`

---

### Complete workflow object

```{r str-complete}
str(complete_result)
```

Typical objects contain:

- `regression`
- `survival`
- `params`
- `metadata`
- `call`

## Logging

Logging can be enabled both in the terminal and with a support file by setting `verbose = 1`
and `save_log = TRUE`:

```{r logging}
run_regression(..., verbose = 1, save_log = TRUE)
run_survival(..., verbose = 1, save_log = TRUE)
run_complete(..., verbose = 1, save_log = TRUE)
```

Minimalist `.log` files containing timestamps and execution steps are written using the
`output_prefix` of each run.

In case `save_log = FALSE`, users can still retrieve the LOG later (regardless of `verbose = 0`)
by running:

```{r write-log}
write_log(file = file.path(out_dir, "my_log.log"))
```

---

## Troubleshooting

The log shows which filters removed features and why a run stopped. Common errors with
the toy data and with real data:

- **"Columns containing only zeros found in input data"**: remove the features that are zero in
all samples before running clinprog.
- **"No signature found: coefficients below threshold"**: no feature reached the minimum average
coefficient. The most common cause for genes is raw expression values with `norm_exp = FALSE`
(use `norm_exp = TRUE`). Other causes are too few bootstrap iterations, or a signal that is
too weak for the sample size.
- **"No signature found: all coefficients are zero"**: usually the filters left fewer
features than `group_size`, so a single regression ran on all of them. Check the line
"columns removed by variance filter" in the log. With `norm_exp = TRUE` the variance is computed
after the log2 transformation, which compresses highly expressed features; lower
`variance_filter` (for example to `0.001`) or provide more features.
- **A survival check stops the run**: by default clinprog applies filtering and checks related to survival
assumptions, and the message names the check that failed. Review the `OS` and `OS.time` columns, consider
another endpoint, or set `skip_survival_checks = TRUE` to continue anyway (results should then be
interpreted with care).

## Running a full example script

A complete example script is also available within the package:

```{r example-script}
script_path <- system.file("scripts", "run_example.R", package = "clinprog")

script_path
```

This script briefly demonstrates how to run the complete clinprog workflow using example toy data.

---

## Reproducibility

clinprog can save:

- Function calls
- Execution parameters
- Seed value used for the bootstrap resamplings
- Package version and timestamps
- Optional command-line invocation metadata

These metadata are stored within returned objects and exported JSON metadata files, as exemplified
before using `write_metadata()`.

---

## Comprehensive summary report

clinprog can generate a summary report containing:

- Metadata, such as function calls and parameters used
- Basic statistics regarding the input datasets
- Summary tables and figures generated throughout the pipeline

The aim of the report is to help users organize and interpret the analysis, as exemplified before using
`write_report()`. Note that some features may not work correctly because they depend on additional packages
listed in the "Suggests" field of the DESCRIPTION file.

---

## Saving and loading clinprog objects (RDS)

clinprog provides utilities to save and reload complete analysis objects in RDS format. This allows users to:

- Persist long-running bootstrap analyses
- Resume work in later R sessions
- Share complete clinprog results between environments
- Ensure full reproducibility of analytical workflows

### Saving clinprog objects

The function `write_rds()` can be used to save any clinprog object
(`clinprog_signature`, `clinprog_survival`, or `clinprog_complete`) into a compressed RDS file.

```{r write-rds}
write_rds(complete_result, file.path(out_dir, "my_complete_result.rds"))
```

By default, compression is set to `"xz"`, ensuring compact file sizes suitable for large genomic analyses.

---

### Loading clinprog objects

Previously saved clinprog objects can be restored using the function `read_rds()`:

```{r read-rds}
loaded_object <- read_rds(file.path(out_dir, "my_complete_result.rds"))

summary(loaded_object)
```

The function automatically validates that the loaded file contains a valid clinprog object and preserves
its S3 class:

- `clinprog_signature`
- `clinprog_survival`
- `clinprog_complete`

This ensures full compatibility with all downstream methods (print, summary, coef, plot, etc.).

---

## Local shiny app

Users not very familiar with the CLI have the option to load a GUI local shiny app to run analyses. Just run:

```r
run_app()
```

Alternatively, users can download and double-click on the `launchers/run_clinprog.sh` file (Linux; make sure it has exec
permission with `chmod +x` first) [`launchers/run_clinprog.bat` for Windows and `launchers/run_clinprog.command` for Mac].
Users must have R installed on the system (with system PATH set) and install clinprog and all its dependencies.

Do not close either the browser window or the terminal while using the Shiny app.

Note that this facility has more limited features.

---

## Notes

- Runtime depends strongly on the number of bootstrap iterations and dataset size.
- Large values of `bootstrap` (e.g., 10,000) may substantially increase runtime; `n_cores` can be used to
parallelize the bootstrap.
- For exploratory analyses, smaller datasets and bootstrap values are recommended.
- The package is primarily designed for high-dimensional transcriptomic survival analyses.
- Users are encouraged to further investigate the clinprog parameters and the generated signature.
- The bundled toy datasets are simulated for demonstration and testing only. Their signatures
carry no biological meaning.

---

## Main dependencies

Core package dependencies include:

- survival
- survivalROC
- survminer
- penalized
- ggplot2
- OptimalCutpoints
- sjstats

See the DESCRIPTION file for a complete and updated list of dependencies.
